clinicalPearls: Inherited disorder of retinal vascular development in which the peripheral retina fails to vascularise, resembling retinopathy of prematurity but occurring in full-term infants without oxygen exposure
Caused by mutations in Wnt/Norrin signalling genes (FZD4, LRP5, TSPAN12, NDP), with autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive and X-linked inheritance

Hallmark findings are a sharply demarcated avascular peripheral retina and, in advanced disease, temporal dragging of the retinal vessels and macula (dragged disc), falciform folds and tractional retinal detachment
Highly asymmetric and variable, ranging from asymptomatic peripheral avascularity found only on angiography to bilateral tractional detachment and blindness
Fluorescein angiography, especially wide-field, is key to demonstrating the peripheral avascular zone, leakage and abnormal vessels, and to screening at-risk relatives
Neovascularisation from the avascular junction can cause exudation, vitreous haemorrhage and retinal detachment
Management is guided by stage and includes surveillance, peripheral laser ablation or anti-angiogenic and surgical intervention for progressive disease, plus genetic counselling
reference.pathophysiology: Familial exudative vitreoretinopathy results from defective Norrin/Wnt-beta-catenin signalling, which is required for normal development of the retinal and inner-ear vasculature. Mutations in FZD4, LRP5, TSPAN12 or NDP impair this pathway, so the peripheral retina remains incompletely vascularised. The resulting retinal ischaemia drives release of angiogenic factors, producing abnormal new vessels, exudation, fibrovascular proliferation and vitreoretinal traction. Traction can drag the macula and vessels temporally and lead to falciform folds and tractional or combined retinal detachment.
additionalDifferentials: Toxocariasis or other causes of a peripheral retinal mass or traction
additionalInvestigations: Wide-field fluorescein angiography to define the peripheral avascular zone, leakage and neovascularisation
Dilated peripheral fundus examination, often under anaesthesia in infants
Angiographic screening of first-degree relatives who may be subclinically affected
Optical coherence tomography for macular traction and dragging
B-scan ultrasonography when media are opaque
Molecular genetic testing of the Wnt/Norrin signalling genes
redFlags: Signs of tractional or rhegmatogenous retinal detachment requiring urgent vitreoretinal referral
Leukocoria or strabismus in an infant suggesting advanced disease
An affected relative prompting screening of the whole family given variable expressivity
reference.prognosis: Prognosis depends heavily on stage: mild peripheral avascularity may never threaten vision, whereas progression to tractional detachment or falciform folds can cause severe, sometimes bilateral, visual loss; early detection and treatment improve outcomes.
pitfalls: Assuming a normal-looking posterior pole excludes disease when the periphery is avascular
Not screening relatives, allowing progressive disease to be missed in mildly affected family members
Confusing it with retinopathy of prematurity without a birth and oxygen history
Underestimating the asymmetry and failing to examine the fellow eye carefully
